connection: Session 01 built PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain, PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App, and PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.Tests as three independently buildable projects sitting in one solution. Nothing yet says which project is allowed to know about which other one. This session wires that up with dotnet add reference, then asks the harder question a beginner usually skips: why does the arrow point the way it does, and what breaks the moment you reverse it?
objectives: Use dotnet add reference to create a ProjectReference from one project to another.
Read a .csproj's <ProjectReference> element and explain the relative path it contains.
Explain why PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App references PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain, and why PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain does not reference PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App back.
Trace the learner TimeClock solution's dependency graph and explain why PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Infrastructure and PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Web both reference Domain independently.
Describe layering: why general-purpose code sits below the specific consumers that depend on it, and where EF Core and ASP.NET Core will eventually attach to that graph.

visuals.title: Consumer projects point at Domain — nothing points back
visuals.explanation: In this lab, App, Infrastructure, Web, and Domain.Tests each gain their own ProjectReference to Domain. Domain's own .csproj remains independent.

visuals.title: A ProjectReference is one XML element, not a build-system mystery
visuals.explanation: dotnet add reference edits the referencing project's .csproj, inserting a <ProjectReference> that points at the other project's .csproj by relative path. That element is the entire mechanism.

visuals.title: Layering: general-purpose code below, specific consumers above
visuals.explanation: Domain knows nothing about App, Infrastructure, or Web. Each of those three layers is free to depend on Domain, be replaced, or gain siblings (a second console app, a background worker) without Domain ever changing.

visuals.title: Reference, then build — the compiler needs the arrow before it needs the code
visuals.explanation: dotnet add reference must run before PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App can call anything in PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain. Without it, ClockEntry and PayrollService are just unresolved names as far as App's compiler is concerned.

preQuiz.prompt: What does dotnet add src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App.csproj reference src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.csproj actually do?
options: It copies PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain's source files into PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App
It edits PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App.csproj, inserting a <ProjectReference> element that points at PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.csproj by relative path
It merges the two projects into one .csproj
preQuiz.explanation: The command's only effect is an XML edit to the first project's .csproj. No source files move or copy anywhere.

preQuiz.prompt: Why does PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App's .csproj have a ProjectReference to PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain, but PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain's .csproj has no reference back to PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App?
options: Domain is a reusable library; App is one consumer of it, and a library should not depend on any particular consumer
preQuiz.explanation: If Domain referenced App, you could never reuse Domain in a second consumer (like PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Web) without dragging App's code along. The dependency points from the specific thing toward the general thing, never the reverse.

preQuiz.prompt: PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Infrastructure and PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Web both reference PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain, but neither references the other. What does that tell you about the dependency graph?
options: It's broken — every project should reference every other project
It fans out from Domain rather than chaining — multiple independent consumers can each depend on the same general-purpose layer without depending on each other
Infrastructure and Web are actually the same project
preQuiz.explanation: A healthy dependency graph in a layered app often looks like several consumers pointing at one shared, lower layer, with no edges between the consumers themselves.

concept.title: dotnet add reference edits one XML element
paragraphs: dotnet add <project> reference <other-project> is a small, literal operation: it opens the first project's .csproj and inserts a <ProjectReference Include="..."/> element whose path points at the second project's .csproj. That relative path is what lets the compiler find the other project's public types when it builds.

After you run the App-to-Domain command, open PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App.csproj and inspect the new ProjectReference. The ..\ segment means go up from App's project folder and then enter its Domain sibling. Domain.Tests sits one directory deeper, so its generated relative path must travel farther.
concept.code:
dotnet add src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App.csproj reference src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.csproj

<!-- resulting element inside PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App.csproj -->
<ItemGroup>
  <ProjectReference Include="..\PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain\PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.csproj" />
</ItemGroup>

concept.title: The direction of the arrow is a design decision, not a default
paragraphs: Nothing about the dotnet CLI forces references to point a particular way — dotnet add reference would happily wire Domain to point at App if you told it to, and the solution would still build. The direction is something you choose, and choosing wrong doesn't fail loudly; it just quietly limits what the code can do later.

PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App references PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain because App is one specific consumer of the domain's types (Employee, ClockEntry, PayrollService) — it's a console program that happens to use those types to do something. PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain never references PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App back, because Domain's job is to be reusable by any consumer, not just this one. A library that reached into its own consumer's code would only ever be usable by that one consumer — every future project that wanted Domain's types would be forced to compile App's console-specific code too, whether it needed a console at all or not.

concept.title: The dependency graph fans out from Domain
paragraphs: The lab creates four independent arrows into Domain: App needs business types for console workflows, Infrastructure will need them for persistence, Web will need them for HTTP delivery, and Domain.Tests needs them to verify domain behavior. None of those reasons requires one consumer to reference another.

The test project references only Domain at this stage because that is all it tests so far. Later, a solution may add separate Infrastructure, Web, or integration test projects rather than turning one test project into a dependency on everything.

concept.title: Layering: where EF Core and ASP.NET Core will eventually sit
paragraphs: "Layering" just means organizing projects so general-purpose code sits below the specific things that use it, and dependencies only ever point downward. Domain is the bottom layer here: it knows about business rules (an employee, a clock entry, a payroll calculation) and nothing about how those things get displayed, stored, or served over HTTP.

App, Infrastructure, and Web are the layer above — each one adds one specific capability on top of Domain without Domain ever needing to know it exists. Later sessions add real behavior to Infrastructure (EF Core, talking to an actual database) and Web (ASP.NET Core, handling HTTP requests), but the layering decision is already made: neither of those technologies will ever leak into Domain's .csproj as a dependency, because Domain has to keep working for every consumer, including ones that don't use a database or an HTTP server at all.

lab.objective: Wire the learner solution's project references with dotnet add reference, inspect the resulting .csproj files, and confirm the dependency graph fans out from Domain with no cycles.
lab.startingCondition: Continue in the same learner workspace from Session 01. It contains all five scaffolded projects, but the projects do not reference each other yet.

steps.text: From the learner workspace root, add the App-to-Domain reference.

steps: Open the resulting PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App.csproj and find the new <ProjectReference> element; note the relative path and confirm it matches src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain's location on disk

steps.text: Add Domain references from Infrastructure, Web, and Domain.Tests, then build the whole solution.
steps.code:
dotnet add src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Infrastructure/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Infrastructure.csproj reference src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.csproj
dotnet add src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Web/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Web.csproj reference src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.csproj
dotnet add tests/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.Tests/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.Tests.csproj reference src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.csproj
dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln

steps.text: Temporarily add the reverse Domain-to-App reference. Confirm it succeeds and the solution still builds, then explain why compiling does not make this dependency direction a good design.
steps.code:
dotnet add src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.csproj reference src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App.csproj
dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln

steps.text: Remove the temporary reverse reference so Domain has no outgoing project references.

steps: Open the App, Infrastructure, Web, and Domain .csproj files in the learner workspace; confirm App, Infrastructure, and Web reference Domain while Domain references none of them.

steps.text: List the projects and draw the reference graph on paper or in a notebook: App, Infrastructure, Web, and Domain.Tests point to Domain; Domain points to none of them.

lab.expectedBehavior: The persistent learner solution builds with App, Infrastructure, Web, and Domain.Tests referencing Domain. The temporary reverse reference from Domain to App compiles but is removed before finishing the lab. Domain ends with no outgoing project reference.

expectedFiles.why: Publish the dependency-direction lesson, lab, and quizzes, expanded from the material moved out of session-01.json.

commit: session-02: wire project references and establish dependency direction
review: The learner solution builds with App, Infrastructure, Web, and Domain.Tests referencing Domain.
The reverse Domain-to-App reference was created, observed to compile, explained as a design mistake, and removed.
The learner workspace's App, Infrastructure, and Web .csproj files each contain exactly one ProjectReference, to Domain.
The learner workspace's Domain.csproj contains no ProjectReference to any other project in the solution.
The dependency graph was described in terms of direction (which project depends on which), not just which files reference which.

postQuiz.prompt: If you accidentally added a ProjectReference from PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain to PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App, what would break first?
options: A future second consumer of Domain (like PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Web) would compile Domain, and transitively compile all of App's code too, even though it never asked for App
The solution file would fail to parse
postQuiz.explanation: A reference pulls in everything the referenced project needs to compile. A library referencing its own consumer forces every future consumer to drag that first consumer along.

postQuiz.prompt: Why does PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.Tests reference Domain at this stage?
options: It needs access to the domain behavior it will verify
Every test project must reference every source project
postQuiz.explanation: A test project points toward the code it verifies. Domain never references the test project back.

postQuiz.prompt: PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Infrastructure will eventually add real EF Core database code. Based on this session's layering discussion, should PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain gain a reference to PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Infrastructure once that happens?
options: Yes, so Domain can use EF Core types directly
No — Domain stays technology-agnostic; Infrastructure depends on Domain, not the other way around, exactly like App and Web already do
Only if the database is SQLite
postQuiz.explanation: Adding EF Core to Infrastructure doesn't change the direction of the arrow. Domain still shouldn't know Infrastructure exists, for the same reusability reason it doesn't know App exists.

reflections: You proved the reverse reference (Domain to App) compiles. Why is "it compiles" not sufficient evidence that a dependency direction is correct?
If TimeClock gained a second console app tomorrow (say, a batch-report generator), what would that new project's .csproj need to reference, and what would stay completely unchanged?
Why does a dependency graph that fans out from one shared project (Domain) tend to be easier to reason about than one where every project references every other project?
whatBreaks: Reversing the reference direction (Domain referencing App) compiles today, because nothing in the .NET toolchain enforces which way project references should point — but it silently blocks every future project, like PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Infrastructure or PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Web, from depending on Domain without also depending on App and everything App needs. Skipping dotnet add reference entirely leaves PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App unable to resolve ClockEntry or any other Domain type, and the compiler reports it as a missing type rather than a missing reference — a genuinely confusing error if you don't already know references are the fix. Letting a non-test project reference PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.Tests would invert the one relationship that's supposed to stay one-directional in the other direction: tests may depend on everything, but nothing may depend on tests.
summary: dotnet add reference performs one concrete edit — inserting a <ProjectReference> element with a relative path — and that element is the entire mechanism behind project dependencies in .NET. The direction those references point is a design decision the tooling will happily let you get wrong: PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App, PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Infrastructure, and PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Web each reference PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain because they are specific consumers of general-purpose code, and Domain references none of them so it stays reusable by all three, and by whatever consumer comes next.
